title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is one of training-data sourcing: an AI music generation system was alleged to have been built using copyrighted recordings without the rights holders' authorization. This is a data-pipeline problem, occurring before deployment, at the point where large volumes of audio material were gathered to train the model. Catching it would have required a systematic audit of every recording in the training corpus against licensing status before training began.

The legal picture is layered and unresolved. Universal Music Group settled and moved to a licensing arrangement. Warner Music Group did the same. Sony Music filed a separate lawsuit alleging the training corpus included over 30,000 of its recordings, and a court declined to let Sony expand its original case, leading it to file a new one. A class action by independent artists survived a dismissal attempt and was transferred to a different jurisdiction. A musicians' union lawsuit over the UMG settlement is also pending. None of these cases has produced a final verdict, and the allegations of infringement are not established findings.

What is established is that training an AI system on commercially released music, without confirmed licensing, created significant legal exposure across multiple rights holders simultaneously. The settlements that did occur required Udio to shift to an opt-in, licensed model going forward, which implicitly acknowledges that the prior approach was not built on that foundation.

summary:
Universal Music Group has reached a settlement with AI music startup Udio, ending a lawsuit that accused Udio of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence model. The agreement includes licensing deals that will allow Udio to launch a new platform next year using only authorized and licensed music. UMG had claimed that Udio improperly used songs like The Temptations' "My Girl" to generate similar compositions without permission or payment to artists and songwriters.

Under the settlement terms, artists can opt into Udio's new platform and will receive compensation, though specific financial details and participating artists have not been disclosed. This marks Udio's first licensing agreement with a major music label. Udio's CEO stated the collaboration demonstrates how AI can empower artists and fans while respecting intellectual property rights. The company, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, has attracted millions of users since launch and counts backing from music artist will.i.am and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.
